UQ Gatton trials cancer drug that could cure dogs with terminal tumours
Date: Mon Feb  9 01:00:00 2026 UTC

UQ Gatton Professor Rachel Allavena said the drug Enzistat developed by American pharmaceutical company Avammune has the potential to treat cancers in dogs and humans. "It gives dogs in southeast Queensland another option, and it's always nice to do cutting edge trials," she said. "The early data that the company has is that it's helped dogs survive longer and have less bad side effects from their cancer. "We're quite hopeful that for dogs that might not have a lot of options that it might be a useful drug in the future." UQ is looking for 30 dogs with inoperable tumours and 30 dogs in palliative care to be part of the trial. Professor Allavena said they hope the drug can shrink inoperable tumours so they could be removed surgically and give a final hope for dogs in palliative care. "They don't have hope for a cure any other way, but their owners just want to see if they can keep them to be around a little longer and see if it can make them more comfortable," she said. She said a third to a half of dogs will get cancer and it is more common than in lots of other species. Professor Allavena has been researching immune-based cancer therapies for about 15 years and she said it was really hard at times. "It's really hard when we hear about one of our patients passing away," she said. "We do also get a lot of joy from giving people hope or giving the animals options." Anyone interested in joining the trial need a cancer diagnosis and referral from their vet. People involved in the trial would need to give a tablet to their dog twice a day for six weeks and need to come to UQ Gatton three times throughout the trial. The medication and any additional blood tests, biopsies, or examinations are provided as part of the study and owners have to cover any other veterinary costs. Contact uqvets.sa@uq.edu.au to join the trial.

Founders Fund invests $4m in Gamgee, Rosie the dog’s AI cancer legacy
Date: Sun Aug 23 06:55:00 2026 UTC

The touching tale of puppy love convinced Founders Fund - which raised capital for OpenAI, Spotify, Facebook and Airbnb - to hand $4m in seed funding to Sydney engineer Paul Conyngham to set up a veterinary biotech company named Gamgee. The extraordinary investment - which followed Mr Conyngham's lunch with OpenAI founder Sam Altman - will allow Gamgee to conduct clinical trials on up to 50 more cancer-stricken canines in Australia this year. "I would never have believed in 1000 years that my little dog would have such a huge impact,'' he told The Australian from the US, where he has hired seven staff for his start-up. "It's been a wild ride to get this far. Founders Fund has backed some of the biggest companies on earth. I feel like this is a natural continuation of Rosie's legacy.'' How Sydney tech entrepreneur, Paul Conyngham, used artificial intelligence to create the world's first personalised mRNA cancer vaccine for his rescue dog, achieving remarkable tumour shrinkage that has astounded leading scientists. Founders Fund partner Amin Mirzadegan said he had been impressed by Mr Conyngham's "rare determination''. "What drew us to Paul was his love of Rosie - it led him to teach himself entirely new fields and push forward where most people would have stopped,'' the venture capitalist told The Australian. "That kind of determination is rare, and it's exactly what we look for in a founder. It also speaks to how AI is beginning to push the ball forward on science.'' Mr Conyngham's dogged use of artificial intelligence to devise an experimental cancer treatment for his pet dog Rosie convinced scientists from the University of NSW to help him sequence the DNA in Rosie's tumours to create a personalised mRNA vaccine to treat the dog's mast cell cancer, after chemotherapy had failed. University of Queensland veterinary researcher Professor Rachel Allavena then treated Rosie with the experimental vaccine, using pre-existing ethics approvals. Although the vaccine shrunk Rosie's tumours, she had to be ­euthanised in June at the age of nine, after one tumour grew back aggressively. "The AI extended her life by two years,'' Mr Conyngham said. "We had the cancer relatively contained until that point but something happened that caused the cancer to wake up and become extremely aggressive. "I don't know what happened, but the cancer came back very aggressively post-surgery - it was very sad to see.'' Mr Conyngham has named his start-up company Gamgee, after the Lord of the Rings character Samwise Gamgee - whose wife is named Rosie. He decided it was "an insanely cool name for this company''. So far he has hired seven staff - biologists, coders and marketers - to launch the new vet biotech company. Mr Conyngham said he was negotiating with University of Queensland to gain ethics and regulatory approval to replicate Rosie's treatment in a multi-site clinical trial involving between 30 and 50 dogs stricken with mast cell skin cancer or bone cancer, before the end of this year. He said he hoped to involve veterinarians along the eastern seaboard. Treatment, which would be free for owners, would involve taking a tissue sample from a dog's tumour, sequencing the DNA and then creating a customised immunotherapy treatment for injection back into the dog.

【turn1065news25】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 2 months ago; Paul Conyngham, an Australian tech entrepreneur, has launched a startup named Gamgee that aims to develop personalized mRNA cancer vaccines for dogs, inspired by his own dog Rosie’s battle with cancer. He claims to have used AI tools like ChatGPT and computational genomics to craft a vaccine that led to shrinkage in Rosie's tumors. Though Gamgee focuses on pet care, its broader ambition extends to personalized treatment for various species, including humans.

Rosie’s case, which features prominently in Gamgee’s marketing, has drawn skepticism from experts who question the scientific validity of the claims, noting that Rosie received multiple treatments, making it unclear if the mRNA vaccine caused her improvement. Despite scientific uncertainties, Gamgee has received backing from Y Combinator and is preparing for clinical trials in Australia, with global recruitment underway. The company promises a simple, quick process for veterinarians and highlights promising initial results, though based on a single case.

Gamgee is collaborating with Australian universities and aims to scale its personalized medicine approach, although its foundation rests on unverified anecdotal outcomes.
Several of her tumours shrank." 
Conyngham, who stresses on Gamgee's website that he is "not a biologist," credits that intervention with adding years to Rosie's life. Gamgee's stated mission is to do that at scale. In case the canine element is lost on its visitors, the website features a slideshow of adorable dogs alongside ages and purported cancer diagnosis to remind them "who we're building this for."
But as I reported for The Verge earlier this year, the science behind Rosie's story is considerably messier than Conyngham's neat account suggests. The exact role AI played in the endeavor wasn't clear, and researchers said the broad claims gave the technology too much credit while minimizing the role of the humans involved. Moreover, the protocol Rosie followed made it impossible to say whether the mRNA vaccine was responsible for her improvement, since it was administered alongside another therapy. 
That hasn't stopped the idea from attracting support. The startup is backed by storied tech incubator Y Combinator and says it is recruiting for its first clinical trials in Australia, with a waitlist open everywhere else (though Conyngham says they're "accepting cases globally."). On a section on its website aimed at veterinarians, Gamgee touts a roughly 75 percent tumor reduction in its "first documented case," while promising to require less than 20 minutes of a veterinarian's time, no new clinical workflows, and a finished "vaccine in hand" in around four weeks. The company cautions that this timeline is based on a single case and may vary. Costs aren't disclosed on the site. 
Gamgee says it's working in collaboration with the University of Queensland and institutes at the University of New South Wales in Australia, and Conyngham encourages potential funders or study partners to reach out. 
Ultimately, the company says its mission extends beyond dogs and other animals to personalized treatments for humans. For a startup built around a single dog whose improvement cannot be clearly attributed to the treatment at the core of its pitch, that's a grand ambition.

【turn1065news26】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 7 months ago; In a groundbreaking medical development, Sydney tech entrepreneur Paul Conyngham used artificial intelligence and mRNA technology to create a customized cancer vaccine for his rescue dog, Rosie. Diagnosed in 2024 with an aggressive mast cell tumor, traditional chemotherapy and surgery failed to stop the cancer. Determined to save her, Conyngham used ChatGPT and AI data processing to analyze Rosie's genomic data, identify cancer mutations, and design a personalized mRNA vaccine with help from experts at the University of NSW.

Developed in collaboration with the UNSW RNA Institute and administered by veterinary researchers at the University of Queensland, the vaccine significantly shrank one of Rosie's large tumors. This marks the first known case of a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine being developed for a dog. The success has inspired optimism among oncologists working on similar treatments for humans, highlighting the potential of citizen-led science and AI applications in medicine. Rosie's improved health underscores the promise of mRNA technology in personalized cancer care, both for animals and potentially humans. Mr. Conyngham is now working on developing a second vaccine to target remaining tumors.
"It raises the question, if we can do this for a dog, why aren't we rolling this out to all humans with cancer? It gives hope to a lot of people, and it's something we're passionate about trying to chase up here.'' 'We often get oddball queries' In a tale of tenacity, Mr Conyngham used a chatbot to brainstorm possible cures for Rosie's cancer - then harnessed artificial intelligence to process gigabytes of genetic data to create the blueprint for an mRNA vaccine. How Sydney tech entrepreneur, Paul Conyngham, used artificial intelligence to create the world's first personalised mRNA cancer vaccine for his rescue dog, achieving remarkable tumour shrinkage that has astounded leading scientists. Harnessing some of Australia's most sought-after scientists to manufacture the vaccine in laboratories at the University of NSW, he then tracked down the only veterinary researcher with ethics approval to administer the experimental drug. It was ChatGPT that suggested immunotherapy, pointing Mr Conyngham to the UNSW Ramaciotti Centre for Genomics, where Associate Professor Smith still remembers the "weird" request. "We often get oddball queries, and this one was coming from a private individual looking to sequence his dog,'' he recalls. "DNA sequencing is a way to profile the tumour and identify mutations that might be causing the disease.'' The renowned researcher was reticent. "Usually we don't support direct-to-consumer type DNA sequencing because while generating data for genomics is relatively easy for us, interrogating that data is really hard and challenging,'' he said.

Yale-developed canine cancer vaccine shows promise for dogs, doubling survival rates (https://www.nhregister.com/news/article/ct-yale-dogs-canine-cancer-vaccine-mamula-therapy-20804986.php)
【turn1065news28】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 1.2 years ago; A promising canine cancer vaccine developed by Dr. Mark Mamula and his team at the Yale School of Medicine is showing significant success in extending the lives of dogs diagnosed with aggressive cancers like osteosarcoma. The vaccine, currently in clinical trials conducted by Mamula’s company TheraJan, targets protein families such as EGFR/HER2, which are responsible for tumor growth. By blocking these proteins and initiating a strong immune response that kills tumors, the vaccine has doubled 12-month survival rates when combined with standard treatments like surgery and chemotherapy—from 30–40% to 60–70%.

The vaccine gained attention following the remarkable recovery of Ranger, a golden retriever previously given little chance of survival. After receiving the vaccine, his cancer ceased progressing and disappeared from scans. Over 11 clinical trial sites across the U.S. are offering the treatment, free of charge, to eligible dogs. The vaccine is pending approval from the USDA and is expected to become the most affordable cancer treatment for dogs on the market. Given the prevalence of cancer in dogs—affecting one in four and half of those over age 10—the vaccine could have far-reaching impact.
